source.title: X-SAM: Boosting Sharpness-Aware Minimization with Dominant-Eigenvector Gradient Correction
source.authors: Hongru Duan; Yongle Chen; Lei Guan

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; no truncation or document mismatch is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains SAM variants and reports test accuracy and sharpness outcomes, using a different intervention to study how optimization relates to generalization. It does not measure the specific behaviors named in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-accuracy comparisons and Hessian-spectrum results for its own X-SAM method and SAM-based comparators. It does not test random-label memorization, width sweeps, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, the optimizer or batch-size comparisons in the versions, dropout, magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, or removal of memorized examples. Figure-only curves are not extracted as numeric rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flatness–generalization premise to develop X-SAM and evaluates its accuracy and Hessian curvature. It does not test any specified version: in particular, raw Hessian eigenvalues and test accuracy do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its ranking of train–test gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase broadly captures the authors' interpretation: eigenvector-based gradient correction constrains dominant curvature and yields superior or comparable accuracy, with non-negligible eigenvector-estimation cost. This should not imply uniform improvement: X-SAM trails GSAM on Fashion-MNIST with WRN-28-10, and the authors' assertion of the highest average on every dataset conflicts with the printed Fashion-MNIST WSAM average.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces intermittent dominant Hessian eigenvector estimation and gradient correction within SAM; uses SGD as the base optimizer. Experiments use image datasets, data augmentation, batch size 256, and 200 epochs.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that X-SAM's test accuracy varies with correction strength α on CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, with α = 0.2 highest among tested settings; it says accuracy is relatively stable for α in [0.1, 0.4].

fits_no_version.finding: X-SAM has higher printed average accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 than the tested SAM variants. Fashion-MNIST results are mixed, and averages use different architecture sets when methods fail to converge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dominant-eigenvector gradient correction within SAM can improve image-classification accuracy relative to the tested SAM variants.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM's second-pass gradient is nearly orthogonal to the dominant Hessian eigenvector for approximately 45% of sampled training observations in a six-layer CNN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM updates can have little alignment with the dominant Hessian eigendirection during training.

fits_no_version.finding: The study reports faster reduction of the largest Hessian eigenvalue with X-SAM and a smaller largest eigenvalue and trace in its spectrum comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: X-SAM can reduce unscaled Hessian curvature measures relative to SAM in the tested settings.

record.problems: The experiments cover three image datasets and four architectures, with three independent repeats, but the text does not provide uncertainty for the reported architecture averages. The paper compares test accuracy and curvature rather than reporting train-test gaps. Several figure results have no numeric values in the text. The Fashion-MNIST table marks two AlexNet method runs as failed to converge.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out from the selected table averages and text-described measurements. Per-architecture values in Table 1 and figure-only curves are not separately extracted; the table averages are reported explicitly, while the plots do not provide textual numeric values.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance under random versus natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, correlation with train–test gaps among similarly fitted networks, and ranking against norm- or margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict applies to V1–V8. Theoretical curvature arguments also do not establish V7's specified empirical association. Section 6.4 names CIFAR-100, but Figure 4's caption and accuracy scale indicate CIFAR-10; that sensitivity result has an unresolved dataset attribution.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning and training recipes.
Large versus small batch sizes and adaptations to training recipes.
Dropout effects and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and its ranking of train-test gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Measure angle between the SAM second-pass gradient and top Hessian eigenvector during training.
rows.value: roughly 45% of the training process: angle between 80° and 100°
rows.note: The paper reports this as an alignment statistic, not as magnitude-aware sharpness or a train-test gap.
rows.check: Subject is a six-layer SimpleCNN, not ResNet-18, according to Section 4.1 and Figure 1. Gradient–eigenvector alignment does not measure V7.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compare largest Hessian eigenvalue through training for SAM and X-SAM.
rows.value: X-SAM decreases faster and exhibits smaller oscillations
rows.note: The text describes the curve comparatively; no numeric values are supplied.
rows.check: Raw largest Hessian eigenvalue is not magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, and no train–test gap ranking is reported. Section 6.2 also calls Figure 2a/2d training losses although their axes and caption identify test losses.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compare Hessian spectra for SAM and X-SAM.
rows.measure: Largest eigenvalue, trace, and eigenvalue concentration
rows.value: X-SAM consistently produces a smaller largest eigenvalue and a smaller trace, with a higher concentration of eigenvalues near zero
rows.note: The paper does not report a train-test gap for this comparison.
rows.check: Timing is internally inconsistent: Section 6.3 says second epoch, while Figure 3's caption says end of training. Raw Hessian spectrum and trace do not measure V7.
